title: Strong foundations. More dependable execution.
source: Your Voice master survey; analysis snapshot 29 October 2026.
notes: Open with the organisational question: how can Safewater Lines preserve what employees value while making everyday work and people decisions more dependable? This presentation describes the supplied response pool, then proposes a bounded pilot. The title is a working interpretation of the evidence, not a measured causal model. Use the dashboard for questions, rather than walking through every metric. Presentation date is 30 October 2026 at TISS. Team names were not supplied, so no names or commitments have been invented.

title:
Preserve pride. Improve coordination.
Make people decisions clearer.
notes: Lead with the recommendation. First protect the positive foundation: pride and own-team support. The first selected improvement priority is cross-team execution; 45 paired records show favourable own-team support and a 1–3 cross-team rating. The second is fairness of people decisions, where consistency, explanations and rewards have lower favourable shares. Recognition, role clarity/backup and visible follow-through support these priorities. These are evidence-informed organising choices, selected with the user, rather than a statistical ranking of causal drivers. The proposed response is a limited 90-day pilot, not an organisation-wide transformation promise.

title: Start with the response base
notes: The master contains 327 response records and 30 complete rating items, giving 9,810 valid rating answers. There are six open-ended questions, 1,892 nonblank comments and 321 records with at least one comment. We have not independently confirmed that each record corresponds to a unique employee. Favourable is 4–5, unfavourable 1–2 and the middle category is Sometimes, not neutral. The culture mean is a custom equal-weight summary of 25 items, excluding overall experience; it is not a validated engagement index. Eligible workforce size is missing, so neither participation rate nor workforce representativeness is established. Qualitative coding remains interpretive and not independently human validated.

title:
Pride and helpful colleagues
are assets to protect
source: item_evidence_profile.csv (PRI2, PRI1, CAM1); employee_voice_topic_summary.csv (preserve topic t).
notes: Three items show a strong foundation: 95.7% understand their contribution to business success, 92.4% are proud to work for Safewater Lines and 91.1% report help within their own team. These are favourable shares of 327 valid answers per item. In the preserve prompt, 119 records mention team or colleague-related strengths. Some identify valued people or relationships rather than describing a specific helpful behaviour, so do not overstate this as 119 accounts of assistance. Keep these strengths as guardrails during the pilot. A higher overall score should not come at the expense of pride or mutual support.

source: survey_clean.csv; five items per block; 1,635 valid answers per block; equal-weight working means.

These block labels come from the questionnaire; naming them does not establish that they are statistically distinct constructs. Means assume equal category spacing and equal weights. We use the distributions and individual questions to guide action rather than assuming that a small difference between means is substantively important. title:
Helpful colleagues do not guarantee
smooth cross-team execution
notes: The own-team support item is 91.1% favourable versus 82.3% for cross-team collaboration, a difference of 8.9 percentage points. Reliance on colleagues in other teams is 80.1% favourable. The stronger evidence is the paired table: 45 records rate own-team support at 4–5 and cross-team work at 1–3, while 16 show the reverse. Both are favourable in 253 records, and both are 1–3 in 13. The difference points to a coordination question, not proof that any specific team is failing. The survey cannot identify which department pair, workflow step or process causes delays. Verify one real handover path before selecting the pilot.

title:
Consistency and explanations
deserve a closer look
source: fairness_item_deep_dive.csv; fairness_response_breadth.csv; item_evidence_profile.csv; n = 327 per item.
notes: Decision consistency, understanding employee decisions and performance-related rewards are the three lowest favourable fairness items. Equal career opportunities and fair workload distribution score higher. Across the five fairness items, 137 records have at least one response at 1–3 and 97 have two or more. This is a breadth measure across items, not the proportion of employees who have been treated unfairly. Sometimes is included, and the items overlap. The appropriate response is to review how criteria are specified, explained and applied, while retaining positive and no-concern experiences. These findings do not establish discrimination or verified misconduct.

to practical changes
notes: Across the six prompts, a record can contribute to multiple request topics but is counted once within each topic. The largest request topics include communication, recognition/feedback and teamwork. These counts help specify what to test; they do not independently validate the rating results or establish severity. Within 308 nonblank fairness-prompt answers, 67 mention career/learning requests, 66 recognition and 64 communication. There are also 73 no-current-concern replies. These figures deliberately retain contrasting experiences. The contextual coding had a documented same-assistant re-review, not independent human validation. All figures could be refined during that validation.

title:
Three practices can make
the two priorities workable
notes: Recognition and feedback, role clarity/backup, and visible follow-through are useful supporting practices. Recognition has 72.5% favourable answers and 179 unique records requesting recognition or feedback. The topic is broader than awards: it includes useful performance feedback. Roles/processes and workload/boundaries appear in 91 and 78 records respectively; these topics overlap and do not diagnose burnout. Listening and action has 79.8% favourable answers, with 134 records requesting voice or follow-through. These patterns suggest specific management practices to test alongside the two priorities. They are not proven causal mechanisms or an independent statistical ranking of priorities.

title:
Pilot two changes
with clear accountability
source: implementation_roadmap_0_90_days.csv (G0, P1-A/B/C, P2-A/B/C); proposed actions, not approved commitments.
notes: For cross-team execution, the proposed accountable owner is the Operations or functional head. First map one real handover path with both sides, then define required information, receiving owner, acknowledgement, escalation and backup. For fairness, the proposed owner is the HR head with business decision owners. Review existing appraisal, progression and reward criteria, make them accessible, give reasons and establish a clarification or review route. All named roles are proposed, not confirmed appointments. Existing tools should be reused where practical; this is not a request to purchase a new platform. Specific facilities, equipment, respectful-treatment or boundary accounts need confidential verification and appropriate routing.

title:
A 90-day pilot turns
the findings into a decision
source: implementation_roadmap_0_90_days.csv; roadmap_decision_gates.csv; all standards and owners are proposals.
notes: At Day 0 the organisation decides whether to approve the pilot scope, sponsor, owners and capacity. During the first 14 days, collect the operational baseline, select exact pulse items, confirm eligible populations and agree numerical outcome targets. Days 15–30 make the pilot ready: checklist, owners, criteria and feedback/concern processes. Days 31–60 operate and adapt the pilot through weekly exception reviews, checking for administrative burden and actual employee usefulness. Days 61–90 repeat comparable experience questions, compare operational measures and decide whether to scale, adapt or stop. Earlier verification of specific accounts should proceed according to urgency and existing routes.

title:
Measure process quality
and employee experience
source: roadmap_kpi_dictionary.csv; roadmap_decision_gates.csv; whole-study survey references are not pilot baselines.
notes: Use both operational process measures and repeated experience items. Required-field completeness is proposed at at least 95% by Day 60; workflow-specific timeliness targets need the first 14-day log. For fairness, criteria and review-route access is proposed for 100% of pilot roles by Day 30, alongside documented reasons for reviewed decisions. These standards are design choices, not effects predicted from the survey. Recognition should track offers, completions and voluntary declines in feedback conversations. Normal concerns should have acknowledgement within two business days, and an owner/next-update date within five; this is not a five-day resolution promise. Repeated item outcomes need comparable wording, composition, valid denominators and nonresponse reporting. Preserve PRI1 and CAM1 as guardrails. Before-and-after change alone is not proof of causality.

title:
Approve a focused pilot,
then scale on evidence
notes: Close with three specific decisions. Approve the scope of one cross-functional workflow and a defined set of pilot roles; name the sponsor and accountable functional/HR owners; and authorise the 14-day baseline effort with a Day-90 review. Numerical outcome targets, capacity and owners still need organisational approval. Protect pride and helpful relationships while improving how work crosses teams and how people decisions are explained and applied. The dashboard supports discussion and the appendix contains the measurement and method detail. Invite discussion on which workflow is most valuable to verify first, rather than asking leadership to endorse a broad unbounded programme.

title: Methods were selected for the decision
notes: Primary evidence is counts, distributions, favourable shares and paired comparisons. Working means assume equal category spacing and weights. The notebook also uses alpha as an internal-coherence diagnostic, exploratory Spearman correlations and selected Kruskal–Wallis comparisons with Benjamini–Yekutieli adjustment. None establishes validity or causation. HR-choice asymptotic p-values were withheld because of sparse cells. Comment analysis uses 15 explicit overlapping topics plus stance/status; it is codebook-based thematic content analysis, not independently validated reflexive thematic analysis. Exact bigrams/trigrams help navigate recurring phrases but do not replace contextual interpretation. The VOSviewer-inspired map describes same-answer co-mentions, with prompt and parameter sensitivity. The specific equal-weight fuzzy construction adds no information over the ordinary mean, so it is not a decision model in the final story.

title:
Keep the results and
their limits together
notes: Primary results retain all supplied records. Excluding identical-category respondents changes the sample; it is not a correction to a known unbiased truth. The selected item shares fall after exclusion, while Pride remains the highest block and Fairness the lowest. The count of 45 paired discordant records cannot include straight-liners by definition, so its unchanged count is not independent robustness evidence. The qualitative re-review covered 568 unique comments, including all 104 original flags, and changed 53 assignment/status decisions. There are 75 remaining cases needing context confirmation, not simply unread comments. No independent human coder or inter-rater reliability is claimed. Selected revised request counts are career/learning 136, fairness 114 and support/respect 139.

title:
Use group patterns to guide listening,
not to assign blame
source: focused_group_profile.csv; cross_team_fairness_overlap.csv; whole-study n = 327; selected groups n ≥ 10.
notes: The 3–5-year tenure group and Customer Service are examples for further listening, not a ranking of problem groups. Eleven of 53 responses in the 3–5-year group show favourable own-team support and a 1–3 cross-team rating; 27 have at least one fairness item at 1–3. Corresponding Customer Service counts are 10 of 51 and 29 of 51. Departments and tenure groups overlap, so they are not independent comparisons. Composition, selection, role mix and working context could explain patterns. The heterogeneous Other grouping is unsuitable for a simple team-level diagnosis. Cross-team and fairness patterns overlap for 47 records but 90 records have a fairness item at 1–3 despite favourable cross-team collaboration, which is why the two priorities should not be collapsed into one explanation.

title: The topic map helps organise discussion
notes: The full primary network includes 1,230 topic-coded suggestion/mixed answers from 305 response records, 13 displayed topics and 34 links supported by at least ten answers. Communication and teamwork co-occur in 98 answers from 93 records; 85 of those answers arise from the teamwork prompt. Fairness and career co-occur in 46 answers from 43 records; 41 come from the fairness prompt. Prompt dependence and parameter sensitivity limit any claim that the graph independently validates a mechanism. Node sizes represent unique-record support within the primary network context, line widths represent answer co-mentions. The offline interactive map provides question exclusion and further context.
